heuristics.rule: Married spouses in Ontario must split property acquired during marriage equally via an equalization payment
heuristics.condition: When a marriage ends for any reason in Ontario
heuristics.action: Calculate each spouse's net family property (property value at separation minus debts and excluded property, minus pre-marriage property value minus pre-marriage debts); the spouse with the larger net family property pays half the difference to the other
heuristics.because: Ontario law requires equalization of net family property upon marriage breakdown — this is not a physical 50/50 asset split but a payment equalizing the financial gain each spouse made during the marriage
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Government of Ontario (ontario.ca) — dividing property when marriage or common-law relationship ends

heuristics.rule: The matrimonial home cannot have its pre-marriage, gift, or inheritance value excluded from the equalization calculation
heuristics.condition: When calculating net family property and one spouse owned the family home before marriage, or received it as a gift or inheritance
heuristics.action: Include the full value of the family home in the equalization calculation — do not deduct the pre-marriage value, gift value, or inheritance value as an exclusion
heuristics.because: Ontario law treats the family home specially: the standard exclusions for pre-marriage property, gifts, and inheritances explicitly do not apply to the matrimonial home
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Government of Ontario (ontario.ca) — dividing property when marriage or common-law relationship ends

heuristics.rule: A court claim for equalization must be brought within 6 years from separation OR 2 years from finalized divorce, whichever comes first
heuristics.condition: When a married spouse in Ontario intends to pursue a court claim for the equalization amount
heuristics.action: File the court claim before the earlier of: 6 years from the date of separation, or 2 years from the date the divorce is finalized
heuristics.because: Missing the limitation period bars the court claim for equalization entirely
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Government of Ontario (ontario.ca) — dividing property when marriage or common-law relationship ends

heuristics.rule: Common-law couples in Ontario have no automatic property division rights regardless of relationship duration
heuristics.condition: When a common-law couple in Ontario separates, regardless of how long they lived together
heuristics.action: Each partner retains only what they individually purchased — no equalization payment or automatic division applies
heuristics.because: Ontario law does not grant common-law partners automatic property-division rights; there is no duration threshold (unlike BC) that triggers such rights
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Government of Ontario (ontario.ca) — dividing property when marriage or common-law relationship ends

heuristics.rule: A cohabitation agreement is the only mechanism for common-law partners in Ontario to establish enforceable property-division terms
heuristics.condition: When common-law partners in Ontario wish to create property rights or obligations between themselves
heuristics.action: Enter into a voluntary cohabitation agreement
heuristics.because: Without a cohabitation agreement, no automatic legal property-division framework applies to common-law couples in Ontario
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Government of Ontario (ontario.ca) — dividing property when marriage or common-law relationship ends

decision_factors.factor: Legal relationship status: married vs. common-law
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether automatic property-division rights exist at all — married spouses have full equalization rights; common-law partners have none automatically
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Establish whether the couple was legally married or in a common-law relationship at the time of separation

decision_factors.factor: Province of residence (Ontario vs. other Canadian provinces)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Property division rules vary dramatically by province — the same fact pattern (unmarried couple, 5+ years together, separating) produces automatic 50/50-equivalent division in BC but zero automatic division in Ontario
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Establish which Canadian province the couple lived in before any property guidance is given

decision_factors.factor: Whether the family home was owned before marriage or received as gift/inheritance
decision_factors.why_it_matters: For all other property, pre-marriage ownership, gifts, and inheritances can be excluded from the equalization calculation; for the matrimonial home, these exclusions do not apply — the full value is always included
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether the property in question is the matrimonial home; if yes, standard exclusions cannot be applied regardless of how it was acquired

decision_factors.factor: Time elapsed since separation and since divorce finalization
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A court claim for equalization is time-barred after 6 years from separation or 2 years from finalized divorce, whichever comes first
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate both: (a) years since date of separation and (b) years since divorce was finalized; the earlier deadline controls

decision_factors.factor: Existence of a cohabitation agreement for common-law couples
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Without a cohabitation agreement, common-law partners in Ontario have no property-division entitlements; with one, the terms of the agreement govern
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether a voluntary cohabitation agreement was signed and whether it addresses property division

decision_factors.factor: Each spouse's net family property (NFP) calculation
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The equalization payment amount is determined by the difference between the two spouses' net family property figures — errors in calculating NFP directly affect the payment owed
decision_factors.how_to_assess: For each spouse: (property value at separation minus debts and excluded property) minus (pre-marriage property value minus pre-marriage debts); the spouse with the higher NFP pays half the difference

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Remaining in a long-term common-law relationship in Ontario without a cohabitation agreement
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Regardless of relationship length, a common-law partner in Ontario acquires zero automatic property-division rights — a partner who contributed financially to the household or property during a decades-long relationship leaves with only what is in their own name
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Common-law partners in Ontario, particularly those who made informal financial contributions to jointly used property titled in the other partner's name

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Owning the family home before marriage and then marrying
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The pre-marriage value of the family home cannot be deducted from the equalization calculation — unlike all other pre-marriage property, the full current value of the matrimonial home is subject to equalization even though the owner brought it into the marriage
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Spouses who owned the family home prior to marriage and assumed they could exclude its pre-marriage value the same way they exclude other pre-marriage assets

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Delaying pursuit of an equalization claim after separation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The limitation period is the earlier of 6 years from separation or 2 years from finalized divorce — divorcing quickly can inadvertently shorten the window for bringing an equalization claim to as little as 2 years from the divorce date
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Spouses who finalize their divorce relatively quickly but then delay pursuing the equalization payment, not realizing the 2-year post-divorce clock may expire before the 6-year post-separation clock

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Assuming Ontario common-law property rules match BC rules because both are Canadian provinces
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: BC has a duration threshold (2 years) after which common-law partners gain automatic property-division rights equivalent to married spouses; Ontario has no such threshold — the rules are opposite in outcome for long-term common-law couples
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Common-law partners who have lived in both provinces or who receive general 'Canadian' advice without province-specific clarification

failure_patterns.pattern: Common-law partner in Ontario attempts to claim automatic property division rights based on relationship duration
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Ontario law contains no duration threshold for common-law partners to acquire automatic property-division rights; the rule in Ontario is a complete absence of automatic division regardless of years together
failure_patterns.consequence: No legal entitlement to any portion of property held in the other partner's name; claim fails entirely absent a cohabitation agreement or other legal instrument
warning_signs: Partner assumes 2-year or other duration threshold applies (a BC rule, not an Ontario rule)
No cohabitation agreement was ever signed
Property was purchased in only one partner's name during the relationship

failure_patterns.pattern: Married spouse in Ontario misses the limitation period for an equalization claim
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The claim must be brought within 6 years of separation OR 2 years of finalized divorce, whichever is earlier — spouses who divorce relatively quickly face a 2-year post-divorce window that may close before they act
failure_patterns.consequence: Court claim for equalization payment is barred; the spouse loses the right to pursue equalization through the courts
warning_signs: Divorce was finalized more than 2 years ago and no equalization claim has been filed
Separation occurred more than 6 years ago and no equalization claim has been filed
Spouse assumed the longer 6-year period always applies without checking whether divorce finalization created an earlier 2-year deadline

failure_patterns.pattern: Spouse incorrectly excludes the pre-marriage or inherited value of the matrimonial home from the equalization calculation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Ontario's standard property exclusions (pre-marriage value, gifts, inheritances) explicitly do not apply to the matrimonial home — applying them anyway produces an incorrect and legally invalid equalization calculation
failure_patterns.consequence: Incorrect equalization payment calculated; if relied upon in a legal proceeding, the calculation will be rejected and corrected to include the full value of the matrimonial home
warning_signs: One spouse owned the family home before marriage and deducts its pre-marriage value in the NFP calculation
The family home was received as a gift or inheritance and treated as excluded property in the calculation

diagnostic_questions.question: Were the parties legally married, or were they in a common-law relationship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether Ontario's equalization framework applies at all — it applies only to married spouses
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If married: proceed to calculate net family property for each spouse and determine equalization payment
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If common-law: automatic property division does not apply in Ontario; ask whether a cohabitation agreement exists

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the couple located in Ontario (as opposed to another Canadian province such as BC)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Province is determinative — Ontario's complete absence of automatic common-law property division is directly contrary to BC's rule; province must be established before any property guidance is given
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Apply Ontario rules: no automatic division for common-law; equalization for married
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Apply the province-specific rules of the relevant province — do not assume Ontario rules apply

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the property at issue include the matrimonial home?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Tests whether the standard exclusions for pre-marriage value, gifts, or inheritances can be applied — they cannot be applied to the matrimonial home
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Include the full current value of the matrimonial home in the equalization calculation without any pre-marriage, gift, or inheritance deduction
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Standard exclusions (pre-marriage value, gifts, inheritances) may apply to the non-home property in question

diagnostic_questions.question: How long ago did the spouses separate, and has the divorce been finalized — and if so, when?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Tests whether the limitation period for an equalization court claim has expired — the deadline is the earlier of 6 years from separation or 2 years from finalized divorce
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If within the limitation period: equalization claim may still be brought; calculate the applicable deadline precisely
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If limitation period has passed: court claim for equalization is barred

diagnostic_questions.question: For common-law couples: did the partners sign a cohabitation agreement, and does it address property division?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether any enforceable property-division terms exist for a common-law couple in Ontario, where no automatic rights exist
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Apply the terms of the cohabitation agreement to determine each partner's property entitlements
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Each partner retains only what is individually in their name — no further property-division entitlement exists under Ontario law

industry_realities.common_belief: In Canada, common-law couples who have lived together for a significant period (e.g., 2+ years) automatically gain property-division rights similar to married couples
industry_realities.actual_reality: This is true in BC (2-year threshold) but explicitly not true in Ontario — Ontario has no duration threshold for common-law couples and provides zero automatic property-division rights regardless of how long the partners lived together
industry_realities.implication: Any person in a long-term common-law relationship in Ontario who has not signed a cohabitation agreement should understand they have no automatic claim to property held in their partner's name upon separation

industry_realities.common_belief: Dividing property in Ontario on marriage breakdown means physically splitting each asset 50/50
industry_realities.actual_reality: Ontario uses an equalization payment system, not a physical 50/50 asset split — each spouse keeps their own property but the spouse who accumulated more net family property during the marriage pays half the difference in NFP to the other spouse
industry_realities.implication: Spouses should focus on accurately calculating net family property figures rather than assuming each individual asset will be divided in half

industry_realities.common_belief: A spouse who owned the family home before marriage, or received it as a gift or inheritance, can exclude that value from the equalization calculation just like other pre-marriage or inherited assets
industry_realities.actual_reality: Ontario law explicitly carves out the matrimonial home from the standard exclusions — the full value of the family home is always included in the equalization calculation regardless of how or when it was acquired
industry_realities.implication: A spouse who brought a home into the marriage or inherited it during the marriage cannot protect that value from equalization the way they could protect, for example, an inherited bank account

industry_realities.common_belief: A separated spouse always has 6 years to bring an equalization claim
industry_realities.actual_reality: The limitation period is the earlier of 6 years from separation OR 2 years from finalized divorce — if the divorce is finalized, the 2-year post-divorce clock may expire well before the 6-year separation clock, eliminating the right to claim
industry_realities.implication: Spouses should not assume the 6-year period applies as a floor; finalizing a divorce quickly can inadvertently reduce the available window for an equalization claim to 2 years from the divorce date

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Applying property-division rules to Canadian common-law couples
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes a duration threshold (e.g., 2 years together) triggers automatic property-division rights for common-law couples across Canada, treating Canadian provinces as uniform
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Immediately asks which province the couple is in before stating any rule — knows that Ontario provides zero automatic division for common-law couples regardless of duration, while BC provides automatic division after 2 years, making province the threshold question
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Giving a common-law partner in Ontario the impression they have automatic property rights could cause them to forgo a cohabitation agreement or fail to take timely legal action, resulting in complete loss of any property claim

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Calculating the equalization payment for the matrimonial home
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Applies the standard pre-marriage value or inheritance exclusion to the family home the same way as any other asset, reducing the equalization base
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Knows the matrimonial home is explicitly carved out of Ontario's standard property exclusions — regardless of pre-marriage ownership, gift, or inheritance, the full current value of the family home is included in the equalization calculation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Incorrectly excluding the matrimonial home's pre-marriage or inherited value produces a lower equalization payment than Ontario law requires, disadvantaging the spouse who is owed the payment

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Advising on the limitation period for equalization claims
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Tells a separated spouse they have 6 years to bring an equalization claim without asking whether a divorce has already been finalized
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Checks both dates — separation date and divorce finalization date — and identifies the earlier of the two deadlines (6 years from separation vs. 2 years from finalized divorce) as the controlling limitation period
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A spouse who finalizes their divorce and then waits more than 2 years to pursue equalization loses the right to a court claim, even if the 6-year separation clock has not yet run
